# Hard-to-vary report: the PRISMA 2020 statement

## 1. The question, frozen

The document answers several. By its title and opening, the central one is: **what should the reporting guidance for systematic reviews be now, and why replace PRISMA 2009 with PRISMA 2020?** Range: systematic reviews of health-intervention effects primarily, extended by statement to other review types and to synthesis-free, mixed-methods, updated and living reviews. What is asked: *does this guidance do its job of making review reports transparent, complete and accurate?* — a design/purpose question with a small causal claim inside it ("advances… necessitated an update"). Frozen here for the test.

## 2. The explanation in parts

**Jobs** (contrast: why *this* and not leaving things alone). **Given by the owner:** users can judge a review's trustworthiness and applicability; an update was needed. **Fixed** (set by the owner, not up for test): 27 items in 7 sections; reporting is addressed, not conduct. **Added by me:** each new item was needed *because* a specific advance made it necessary, not merely preferable; after adoption, the newly required things get reported more completely.

**Change list** (changes to the world it claims to keep matching): new methods (machine learning search, non-meta-analysis synthesis, new bias tools); the shift from "quality" to "certainty"; the publishing landscape (preprints, repositories, registration); and review type (intervention, social, aetiology, prevalence, prognosis; with or without synthesis; original / updated / living). **Left off, and said so openly:** conduct, methodological-quality appraisal, protocols, PRISMA extensions. That is an honest, non-empty list — a point in its favour.

## 3. Part by part

| Part (owner's words) | Mark | By what, or what would settle it |
|---|---|---|
| "To capture these advances… necessitated an update" | Held if | Held only by the added job that a *necessary* update existed; no per-item test is given. Settle by naming the 2009 wording a given advance could not cover. |
| "seven sections with 27 items, some… sub-items" (inherited from 2009) | Loose | The count and the section split could be otherwise. Held part is "each reporting element has a home." |
| Item 2 abstract checklist | Held | Remove it and the job "abstracts are read on their own" fails. |
| Items 15 & 22 certainty of evidence | Held | The quality→certainty shift and users' need to judge trustworthiness. |
| Item 7 full search strategies for *all* sources | Held | Reproducibility. Swap "all sources" for 2009's "at least one" and replication breaks. |
| Item 8 independent screening / automation used | Held | Bias job. Swap "independently" for "how long screening took" — the bias job fails. |
| Items 26, 27 competing interests; data and code available | Held if | Held by a trust-and-reproducibility job the document asserts rather than tests. |
| "Explanation and elaboration" bullet-point "elements" | Loose | Any readable format would do. Held part: "each item comes with its reason and an example." |
| 60 documents; 110/220 respondents; 21 members; two days; five revisions; 15 reviewers | Loose (free) | Swap any count and nothing in the guidance changes. Held part: "several independent kinds of input." |
| "theoretical considerations… and co-authors' experience" | Borrowed (catch-all) | Rests on the co-authors' practice, untested — needs a gauge. |
| "many items are applicable to… aetiology, prevalence, or prognosis" | Held if | Held only by the asserted job that the guideline should stretch to other review types. |
| "effects of only 11 have been evaluated… unclear which strategies should be used" | Held | It states its own gap and a test (randomised trials). |

**Two routes to one job:** *why update at all* is carried by two independent supports — reported incompleteness under 2009, and advances since 2009. Either alone would do; neither is needed alone. Never cut both.

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

- **Flip.** Had reporting been complete and methods static, the parts commit the authors to "no update" — it sticks its neck out. But flip the *origin*: the survey asked respondents whether to "keep, modify, or remove" each item, so it can only return a list of modifications; a process that always outputs "revise" explains neither the timing nor the content.
- **Reverse / direction.** "Advances necessitated an update" runs partly backwards. Poke the supposed cause: more preprint servers do not force item 7. The advance makes an update *plausible*, not *necessary*. The working direction is: an update was decided, then advances were named. That answers "what can we tell?" better than "what produced it?"
- **Answer hidden in the starting points.** "Update needed" sits in the setup: the questionnaire presumes modification is on the table and the meeting's purpose is revision.
- **Add a job (mine).** That adoption actually makes reports more usable to patients and policy makers. The document declines it ("has the *potential* to benefit") and rules out no rival version of itself — so the new job held nothing new in place.
- **Build the best rival.** "An incremental update — mostly finer-grained reporting, plus a few genuinely new items." No listed change cleanly separates it from the stated claim: for the split items, both descriptions fit. They are the same at this level. A finer question would separate them: *which item could not have been written in 2009?*
- **Pull.** Completeness pulls against journal word and section limits; the line is drawn at "put detail in supplementary files or refer to the protocol." What would show the line is misplaced: readers still cannot find what they need to judge bias. Second pull: "adhere to all items" against "the suggested location… should not be prescriptive."
- **Catch-alls and gauges.** "Co-authors' experience" and "other stakeholders" can absorb any item. Gauge needed: name one item that experience — not the evidence review or the survey — put in, and the reading that would drop it. The flow diagram "can be modified": gauge = what must appear in every version.
- **Where the parts came from.** The checklist is **built** (drafted with the reviews and survey in view, revised five times); the retained 2009 items are **fitted** (they survived past use); the development narrative — meeting, revisions, feedback — is **asserted**. Fitted parts cannot be confirmed on the cases they were fitted to; "it has worked since 2009" says nothing about unmet changes.

## 5. What would make it harder to vary

1. For one substantive change (say the certainty items), name the 2009 item text that could not cover it, *and* a change that would have shown a different item was needed. One such case does more than the whole advances list.
2. A gauge for "co-authors' experience": one item only that route contributed, and the reading that would remove it.

## 6. What this does not show

Passing is not truth. This is mostly a design, and the tests cannot settle whether adoption improves reviews — the document agrees, noting only 11 of 31 adherence interventions have been evaluated.

## 7. One next step

Take the certainty-of-evidence item. Write down, before looking, the prediction that pre-2020 PRISMA-compliant reviews reported it less often than an unrelated item (say, number of tables). Then check. A change that should matter, next to one that should not — that is the test the "advances" list never runs.

Now let me apply the method to the PRISMA 2020 statement document.

Freeze the question. The document answers several questions. The title/opening makes central: "The PRISMA 2020 statement: an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews." Opening says systematic reviews serve roles, need transparent reporting, and PRISMA 2009 is the guideline; advances necessitated an update. So the central question the document answers: "Why should PRISMA 2009 be replaced by PRISMA 2020, and what should the new reporting guidance consist of?" I'll frame it as a design/rules + rationale question: What should the reporting guidance for systematic reviews be now, and why the change from PRISMA 2009?

Kind of question: mixed — a design (what should the guidance be / does it achieve its purpose?) and a causal/historical claim (why the update was necessitated). I'll name it. The method says name the kind. It's a design (rules/instructions content) with a rationale. Kind: "Does it achieve its purpose?" / design. Also partly "What produces it?" for the causal claim that advances necessitated the update.

Now list jobs. Contrast-framed jobs:
1. Why update to PRISMA 2009 at all, and not leave it? (given: the doc names this)
2. Why these particular 27 items and changes (e.g., why add certainty assessment, why move protocol/registration) and not others? (added)
3. Why an abstract checklist now — why wasn't it in the main 2009 checklist? (added)
4. Why should a review report X (transparency) — what job does transparency do for users? (given)
5. Does it achieve its purpose — does PRISMA 2020 change reporting? (partly given: "we anticipate... benefit"). 

Change list: what changes to the world does the claim cover? Changes in methods (NLP/ML, new synthesis methods, risk-of-bias tools, terminology shift quality→certainty, publishing landscape like preprints, registration). Changes in the field of application (health interventions vs social/educational vs aetiology/prevalence/prognosis; synthesis vs no synthesis; mixed methods; original vs updated vs living). These are the changes the guideline claims to cover. What's left out: it says explicitly it doesn't guide conduct, doesn't assess quality, doesn't cover protocols (PRISMA-P), extensions cover network meta-analysis etc. It states those limits openly — good.

Parts of the explanation:
A. The update was necessitated by advances (tech NLP/ML, new synthesis methods, new risk-of-bias tools, terminology evolution, publishing landscape). — the causal reason for the update.
B. The seven-section, 27-item checklist with sub-items.
C. The abstract checklist (item 2).
D. The explanation and elaboration (E&E) paper with bullet "elements".
E. Flow diagram templates (original/updated).
F. The development process: reviews of reporting transparency, review of 60 guidance docs, survey (110/220 methodologists+editors), 21-member two-day meeting, 5 revisions, feedback from 15 reviewers.
G. Catch-all: "co-authors' experience with authoring and using systematic reviews" — absorbs judgment.
H. "PRISMA 2020 is applicable to... many items applicable to..." — scope.
I. Adherence strategies list (educators, editors, peer reviewers, etc.) with "effects of only 11 of 31 evaluated... unclear which."

Where each part came from: mostly built/asserted/fitted.

Now run tests.

Remove: remove the "advances necessitated an update" list. Does the update still get justified? Largely yes on other grounds — poor reporting / desire for completeness. Hmm. Actually the specific content changes (certainty items, data availability item) are motivated by advances/trends. If you remove the advance list, the items lose their reason. But the document also says PRISMA 2009 was associated with more complete reporting yet more could be done. So the update has two routes to "why update": (i) advances since 2009, (ii) incomplete adherence. Two routes to one job.

Remove the abstract checklist: is there a job it does alone? It addresses that abstracts are a distinct dissemination channel with their own reporting needs (and updates PRISMA for Abstracts 2013). But could an abstract be covered by "refer to the main checklist"? The document gives it as a separate item with a separate checklist. Is a separate abstract checklist held? Its job: abstracts are read standalone by users. Arguably held by the dissemination job.

Swap: Each checklist item for a near neighbour. E.g., item 8 "study selection — how many reviewers screened, whether independently, automation tools used." Swap "whether they worked independently" for "how long screening took." Does the item still do its job (enable readers to judge risk of bias)? No — independence relates to bias, time does not. So held by the bias job. Good.

Swap a loose one: the number "60 documents", the count of survey respondents (110/220), "21-member, two-day, in-person meeting in Edinburgh." Swap 21 for 25 members: does the guidance still do its job? Nothing in the document's claim changes. These numbers are loose/free. The held part is that a range of stakeholders and evidence sources fed the checklist — more general than the exact numbers.

Flip the outcome: suppose reporting were already transparent and complete and methods hadn't advanced. Would the document have said "no update needed"? The document is built so it could only conclude an update was needed — but that's because it's a case for the update. Flip test: if PRISMA 2009 had already produced complete reporting, would authors still have written a case to update? Under the document's own parts, the update rests on reported incompleteness and advances. So flip seems to bite: it commits to "if completeness and methods were unchanged, no update." That's a real commitment — arguably held. But note the survey and meeting are designed to produce modifications regardless; a mechanism that always outputs "modify" is loose.

Hunt answer in starting points: The conclusion "update needed" — is it in a starting point? "To capture these advances in the reporting of systematic reviews necessitated an update." The advances are given as fact (borrowed from other literature, cited in background). And the need for the update is inferred from those advances plus reported incompleteness. Somewhat circular risk: the modifications were proposed by surveying people who were asked whether to modify — a survey that asks "should we modify or keep/remove" can yield modifications by construction. Also "our recommendations are informed by... co-authors' experience" — a catch-all.

Poke: name a change that should alter the outcome and one that should not.
- Should alter: if a new reporting element turned out to be inconsistently reported across reviews (e.g., certainty of evidence), PRISMA 2020 would include an item on it (item 15, 22). And the guideline predicts: after adoption, reports include the new items. That's testable.
- Should not alter: changing the font, the number of co-authors, the exact meeting city. Those shouldn't change the guidance.
Watch the part: "reporting completeness" — under a change to how completeness is measured (a new instrument), the reading moves; the thing (reporting practice) may not.

Reverse: Is the document running backwards? The causal claim "advances necessitated an update" — direction: did advances produce the update, or did the authors decide to update and then list advances to justify? Evidence: the "noteworthy changes" list was produced after the survey/meeting. Poke the effect: publishing more preprints — does it force item 7 (full search strategies)? No. The advances make an update *plausible*, not *necessary*. So "necessitated" is stronger than what the parts hold. Reverse finding: for many specific changes, the document can't show the advance produced the change; a modification was proposed and an advance named to justify it. That's a fitted/asserted part.

Add a job: if PRISMA 2020 is right, what else must be so? That following the checklist improves the trustworthiness/applicability of reviews to users. Does the doc cover it? It asserts potential benefit ("has the potential to benefit") — hedged. The added job (does adopting the checklist improve outcomes?) is not ruled out, and the document doesn't test it; it says only 11 of 31 adherence interventions have been evaluated. So the added job leaves the explanation unchanged and rules out nothing new → adds little. But it does highlight an untested dependency.

Build the best rival: a rival explanation for the changes: "PRISMA 2020 is mostly an update of wording and a rebranding; the substantive changes are the certainty items and data-availability item." What change tells them apart? If the 27 items are largely the 2009 items reworded, then the "advances necessitated" claim is doing little. Test: count substantively new items vs reworded. The document itself lists noteworthy changes — mostly modifications/splits (reporting more detail) rather than new reporting concepts, plus two or three genuinely new items (certainty, competing interests, data availability). So the rival "mostly more granular reporting, few new concepts" is largely at the same level as the stated claim — no listed change separates them cleanly. Say so, or ask a finer question (which items could not have been written in 2009?).

Pull: parts in tension. "Complete reporting benefits users" vs "journals impose word/section limits" — the document resolves it with "put detail in supplementary files / refer to the protocol." Tension: completeness pulls one way, practical space pulls the other; where it gives way is at supplementary files. Also tension: "adhere to all items" vs "not prescriptive about location." Also "PRISMA improves reporting" vs "effects of adherence strategies mostly unevaluated." 

Check patches: the document's patches — "many items are applicable to..." (scope patch, narrows where the claim holds, openly), "if the relevant information appears in the protocol, referring to it may suffice" (narrowing/fallback), "supplementary files" (escape hatch), "not intended to guide conduct/assess quality" (limits stated openly). The limits are mostly stated openly, which is good. Catch-all: "co-authors' experience" (a bin that can absorb any item) — needs a gauge. Also "other stakeholders" in the benefit list. Also the flow diagram "can be modified depending on whether the review is original or updated" — a flexible template that can absorb anything unless a gauge controls how it's modified.

Look inside: The claim "PRISMA 2020 facilitates reporting that lets readers assess trustworthiness." That's about outputs (reports) not workings (does the review itself improve?). The document is honest it doesn't test that. So the item-level parts can't be tested by output counts alone; need inside changes (do reviewers/editors actually use it; do reports change).

Whole-explanation checks: flip (mostly committed), direction (some reverse), hidden-in-starting-points (mild — the survey assumed modifications were wanted), pairs that pull (completeness vs space; all-items vs not-prescriptive), catch-alls ("co-authors' experience", "other stakeholders") need gauges, change list leaves out (conduct, quality assessment, protocols, extensions — all stated openly), rivals (incremental rebranding), provenance (mostly built from evidence + asserted from consensus).

What would make it harder to vary: (a) for each substantive change, name the change in the world that would have shown it was *not* needed, and the one that would have shown a different change was needed — i.e., what the 2009 guideline could not express. (b) A gauge for "co-authors' experience": which item did experience add that the evidence review and survey did not, and would the item survive without it? (c) A prediction written beforehand: which items will remain under-reported after adoption, testable.
